We need to deduce SMILES given data: formula C11H15O2N, DBE 5, aromatic carbons 6, CH3 groups 2, C=O groups 1, carbon types 9, hydrogen types 6. Fragments: aromatic ring c1ccccc1 (benzene). C(=O)N (amide). CCO (ethanol). C (maybe methyl). Another C (maybe methyl). Need to assemble.

We have aromatic ring (6 carbons). One carbonyl attached to N (amide). Likely an acetanilide derivative? C11H15O2N: Let's think of possible structure: maybe N-acetyl-para-methyl aniline? But formula: C11H15NO2. Let's compute: anilide (C6H5-CO-NH-CH3) would be C8H9NO? Actually anilide: C6H5-CO-NH-CH3 = C8H9NO? Wait count: C6H5 (C6H5) + CO (C1O1) + NH (N1H1) + CH3 (C1H3) = total C8? Actually C6+1+1 =8 carbons, H5+1+3 =9, O1, N1 => C8H9NO. Not match.

Our formula C11H15O2N suggests maybe a phenylacetic acid amide? Let's think: phenyl (C6H5) attached to CH2-CO-NH-CH3? That would be C6H5-CH2-CO-NH-CH3: Carbons: 6+1+1+1 =9? Wait CH2 (C1), CO (C1), CH3 (C1) total C9. Not enough.

Maybe we have aromatic ring with two substituents: one carbonyl amide, one ethoxy? Fragments include CCO (ethanol) maybe ethoxy group attached to aromatic? CCO is -CH2-CH3-O? Actually CCO is ethanol: CH3-CH2-O? In SMILES "CCO" is CH3-CH2-OH. Could be an ethoxy group attached to aromatic via O (phenoxy ethyl). But we have only one O in carbonyl and one O maybe in ether? O2 total.

We have C(=O)N fragment (amide). CCO fragment (alcohol). Two separate C fragments (maybe methyl groups). Aromatic ring.

We need total C=11. Aromatic 6. C(=O)N adds carbonyl carbon (1). CCO adds 2 carbons (CH3-CH2). Two C fragments each 1 carbon = 2. Sum =6+1+2+2=11. Good.

Now need to place them: maybe aromatic ring attached to carbonyl (amide) and also attached to ethoxy group? But we have only one N, one carbonyl O, one ether O. So maybe structure is phenacetyl? Wait phenacetyl is phenyl-CH2-CO-CH3? Not.

Consider "acetanilide" has formula C8H9NO? Not.

Our fragments: C(=O)N (amide) could be attached to aromatic carbon (forming anilide). CCO could be attached to aromatic via O (phenoxy ethyl). Two methyl groups maybe as substituents on aromatic? But we already have CH3 groups counted: there are 2 CH3 groups total. One CH3 is part of CCO (the terminal CH3). Another CH3 could be the separate C fragment (methyl). The other separate C could be maybe attached to aromatic as a substituent (like methyl). So aromatic ring would have substituents: an amide carbonyl (C=O) attached to N (maybe -CONH-CH3?), an ethoxy group (O-CH2-CH3), and a methyl group. That would be 3 substituents on benzene, which would give aromatic carbons 6, plus substituents: carbonyl carbon (1), ethoxy two carbons (2), methyl (1) = total 10? Wait plus maybe the amide N attached to something else? The C(=O)N fragment includes carbonyl carbon and N attached to something else (maybe H). The N may have H (NH). That matches O2 (one carbonyl O, one ether O). So formula: C6H4 (since three substituents replace three H) + substituents: carbonyl carbon (C=O) attached to N-H (no extra carbon), ethoxy group (CH2-CH3) attached via O, methyl group (CH3). Count carbons: aromatic 6, carbonyl carbon 1, ethoxy 2, methyl 1 =10. Need 11. Wait we also have maybe an extra carbon attached to amide N (like N-CH3). But we already used the methyl as separate C fragment; maybe the amide is -C(=O)NCH3 (acetamide). That would add another carbon (methyl attached to N). Then total carbons: aromatic 6 + carbonyl carbon 1 + ethoxy 2 + N-methyl 1 + aromatic methyl 1 =11. Good. So structure: aromatic ring with three substituents: (1) N-methyl amide carbonyl attached to ring (i.e., -C(=O)NCH3) (like acetanilide with N-methyl). (2) ethoxy group attached via O (phenoxy ethyl) -OCH2CH3. (3) methyl group attached directly to ring.

Now check hydrogen count: aromatic ring C6H? With three substituents, aromatic hydrogens = 3 (since benzene has 6 H, each substituent replaces one). So aromatic H =3. Methyl on ring adds 3 H. Ethoxy: CH2 (2 H) + CH3 (3 H) =5 H. N-methyl: CH3 (3 H). Plus maybe NH? The amide N may have H? In N-methyl amide, N attached to carbonyl and methyl, may have H? Actually N-methyl amide would be -C(=O)N(CH3)H? If N has one H, then there is an NH. That adds 1 H. Total H = aromatic 3 + ring methyl 3 + ethoxy 5 + N-methyl 3 + NH 1 =15. Good matches formula H15.

O count: carbonyl O (1) + ether O (1) =2. N count 1. Good.

DBE: formula C11H15NO2 DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 +1 = 11 - 15/2 + 1/2 +1 = 11 -7.5 +0.5 +1 =5. So matches.

Carbon types: need 9 unique carbon environments. Let's see: aromatic carbons: with substituents, there will be maybe 4 distinct types? In a trisubstituted benzene with substituents at positions maybe 1,2,4? Not sure. But plausible 9.

Thus SMILES: need to represent: aromatic ring with methyl, ethoxy, and N-methyl amide carbonyl. Choose positions: e.g., 1-methyl, 2-ethoxy, 4-(N-methylcarbamoyl). SMILES: "Cc1ccc(OCC)cc1C(=O)N(C)". Wait need carbonyl attached to ring: "c1ccc(C(=O)N(C))cc1OCC"? Actually carbonyl attached directly to aromatic carbon: "c1ccc(C(=O)N(C))cc1OCC". Also need methyl on ring: "c1ccc(C)cc1" but we already have methyl as substituent. So combine: "Cc1ccc(C(=O)N(C))cc1OCC". Let's count carbons: methyl attached to aromatic (C) before ring, then aromatic 6, carbonyl carbon (C=O) (1), N-methyl (C) (1), ethoxy two carbons (CC) (2) = total 11. Good.

Check SMILES validity. Use validate tool.
